name: Federation of American Scientists (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: almost all the value is the nuclear and AI work, against risks that kill people everywhere, so the result is spread by world population; the science-policy work (a few percent of the value) is for Americans.
summary: The Federation of American Scientists (Washington DC) counts the world's nuclear arsenals in the open through its Nuclear Information Project, ran a Global Risk Program on AI, nuclear and biological risk, has a small AI safety and security policy team, and spends most of its money on making US science policy and government work better: fellows placed in federal agencies, the Day One Project's policy proposals, research teams on climate, government capacity and data, and nine fiscally sponsored projects. This model covers all its programmes in the year to June 2025 ($36.4M spent). At the defaults it averts about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000, from 0.07 to 29 on the combined range: 93% of that is the nuclear work (about 3% of the cost), valued as a typical project's cut in the forecast risk of nuclear war (Rethink Priorities' cross-cause model, the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's experts), 4% the AI work, 2% the pandemic work and under 1% the science-policy work, valued as better use of US public money at what a dollar is worth to the average American. Only about 5% of its spending is on catastrophic risks. The biggest uncertainty is how much a dollar of nuclear work cuts the risk (Rethink calls its figures placeholders; the range runs ten times either way) and how much of the research spending is the Nuclear Information Project's and the Global Risk Program's. Every branch is discounted for missing data: no outcome of the work is measured.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

rows.label: Discounted future years of healthy life per person of the long-run population, if the future ends now
rows.explainer: The site's one count of future generations (docs/normalization.md 2.19): the healthy years of people not yet born, discounted for ever at the shared rate. People alive now die in the catastrophe and are counted as deaths, so this stream rises from nothing to the long-run population over one lifetime (@catastrophe.life_expectancy_now) and then runs on: about 8 years at the default 4%, about 960 at the 0.1% floor. Fixed; don't edit.

rows.label: AI: deaths averted a year by a typical $1 million of work, while its cut counts
rows.formula: ((1 - ai_misuse_cost_share) * @catastrophe.ai_extinction_cut_per_million + ai_misuse_cost_share * @catastrophe.ai_misuse_extinction_cut_per_million) * ai_extinction_per_year * deaths_if_extinct + ((1 - ai_misuse_cost_share) * @catastrophe.ai_catastrophe_cut_per_million + ai_misuse_cost_share * @catastrophe.ai_misuse_catastrophe_cut_per_million) * (ai_catastrophe_per_year * ai_deaths_if_catastrophe + ai_smaller_per_year * ai_smaller_deaths)
rows.explainer: The share of each yearly risk a typical $1 million of work in the area removes (Rethink Priorities' cross-cause model, its backfire step included; shared), × the deaths that risk carries: misuse work at Rethink's misuse preset, other AI work at its misalignment preset, weighted by ai_misuse_cost_share. The catastrophe figure also applies to the smaller size. Fixed; don't edit.

rows.label: AI: future healthy years kept a year by a typical $1 million of work
rows.explainer: As ai_deaths_per_million, for the future lost in an extinction-level catastrophe: the two presets' extinction cuts weighted by ai_misuse_cost_share.

rows.explainer: The AI safety and security policy team's share of the research line, the Global Risk Program's AI part (autonomy, cyber, AI generally) and the Day One proposals on catastrophic risks, over all programme spending; overhead is spread alike. FAS's other AI work (AI in government services, data governance) is government capacity, in the gov branch.
rows.formula: (research_line * (ai_staff_share + global_risk_share * (1 - gr_nuclear_share - gr_bio_share)) + dayone_line * dayone_gcr_share) / program_spend

rows.explainer: Everything else, about 97% of the cost: the nine fiscally sponsored projects (the Alliance for Learning Innovation, which campaigns for federal education research and development, the largest), the talent initiatives (fellows in the Department of Agriculture and other agencies, and ten in civil society on energy affordability, digital government and federal data), the rest of the Day One Project and the Center for Regulatory Ingenuity, and the issue teams on climate and energy, wildfire and heat, government capacity, federal data and state and local government (MetroLab Network). rows.label: Science policy and government capacity: public money a year in the programmes the work touches, per dollar spent
rows.explainer: The yearly public budgets whose use a dollar of the work bears on: fellows placed inside Department of Agriculture programmes worth billions a year, Day One proposals for federal agencies (the CHIPS and Science Act, about $280 billion, "includes policy ideas from more than a dozen memos authored for the original Day One project", FAS 2025 annual report, https://a-fasannualreport2025.vev.site), wildfire and heat policy (federal wildfire spending runs to billions a year), the Alliance for Learning Innovation's case for federal education research (the Institute of Education Sciences, under $1 billion a year). About $30M a year of work bearing on some $3 billion of public money a year: 100 dollars per dollar, from 10 to 1,000, our judgment.

rows.label: Share of public investment's value lost to inefficiency, advanced economies
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for how much better public spending in rich countries could do (the IMF's efficiency gap for public investment, facts/democracy.json): the room the work can close. It is measured on investment and applied here to all the public spending the work touches, programmes and regulation too, for want of a figure for those; gov_gap_closed's wide range covers the difference.

rows.label: Science policy and government capacity: share of that gap the work closes in the programmes it touches, a year
rows.explainer: Most proposals aren't adopted and a fellow is one person in a large programme, so the work closes a small part of the gap: 2% (0.2% to 10%), our judgment. With gov_public_dollars_per_dollar and gov_efficiency_gap, a dollar of the work adds about 26 cents of public value a year, about $1.2 over the years counted: a science-policy dollar worth about what it costs in the US public good it buys, from far less to over ten times.

rows.label: Science policy and government capacity: years from the spending until programmes change
rows.explainer: A proposal taken up or a fellow's change made takes about a year, our judgment, 0 to 3, as the catastrophic-risk branches; discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Science policy and government capacity: discounted years a change counts
rows.explainer: A change in how a programme works counts the site's years for a won reform ($win_years_counted), after its wait, at the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Value of a dollar of US public good, in units of value
rows.explainer: A dollar more of what public money buys for Americans, valued like a dollar of consumption to the average American: one over the household survey's consumption per person (the Consumer Expenditure Survey, 2024, in 2025 dollars: the one scale for US public money, docs/normalization.md 2.14) in ln(consumption), × the shared value of doubling consumption. No marginal cost of public funds: better use of the same money costs the payers nothing more.

rows.label: Science policy and government capacity: better public spending, in units of value (before adjustments)
rows.formula: cost_total * gov_cost_share * gov_public_dollars_per_dollar * gov_efficiency_gap * gov_gap_closed * gov_discounted_years * gov_value_per_public_dollar
rows.explainer: The branch's cost × public money touched per dollar × the share of its value lost to inefficiency × the share of that the work closes × the discounted years × the value of a dollar of US public good. Enters the result through the bridge from units of value (uov_bridged).

rows.label: Check: the cost shares add up to all the modelled spending
rows.formula: ai_cost_share + bio_cost_share + nuclear_cost_share + pol_cost_share + fb_cost_share + gov_cost_share
rows.explainer: Must be 1: every dollar of the modelled programme is in exactly one branch.

rows.label: Deaths averted, every branch (expected, before adjustments)
Deaths averted that are in a COVID-scale pandemic (a part of deaths_averted)
rows.explainer: A natural or zoonotic pandemic on COVID's scale kills mostly older people, so its deaths are valued at COVID-19's age mix; every other size (a catastrophe that kills a share of the world, extinction) at the world's. A policy or field-building branch pointed at the pandemic area adds its deaths averted × bio_covid_scale_share here. Fixed.

rows.label: Value of a death averted in a COVID-scale pandemic (units of value)
rows.explainer: As value_per_death, with the shared COVID-scale age mix (@death_ages.covid_scale_*): the one value of a death by age. Fixed.

rows.label: Future healthy years kept, every branch (expected, before adjustments)
Healthy years per unit of value of the deaths averted (for the weights below)
rows.explainer: The bridge's healthy years per unit of value, times the losses beyond deaths that only the deaths carry: turns each branch's deaths into healthy years for the weights. Written over uov_bridged because the gov branch's units of value go through the same bridge.

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from the AI work (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The branch's deaths averted in healthy years, plus its future healthy years kept: the weight its adjustments carry. Fixed.

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from the pandemic work (before adjustments)
rows.formula: bio_deaths_averted * ((1 - bio_covid_scale_share) * value_per_death + bio_covid_scale_share * covid_value_per_death) * dalys_per_death_value + bio_future_dalys
rows.explainer: The branch's deaths averted in healthy years (the COVID-scale part at COVID-19's age mix), plus its future healthy years kept: the weight its adjustments carry. Fixed.

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from the nuclear work (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The branch's deaths averted in healthy years, plus its future healthy years kept: the weight its adjustments carry. Fixed.

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from the policy win (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The branch's deaths averted in healthy years (a policy or field-building branch pointed at pandemics: its deaths at w_bio's mix, as in covid_scale_deaths_averted), plus its future healthy years kept: the weight its adjustments carry. Fixed.

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from the people trained (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The branch's deaths averted in healthy years (a policy or field-building branch pointed at pandemics: its deaths at w_bio's mix, as in covid_scale_deaths_averted), plus its future healthy years kept: the weight its adjustments carry. Fixed.

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from the science-policy and government-capacity work (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The branch's units of value in healthy years: the weight its adjustments carry.

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from every branch (before adjustments)
rows.formula: w_ai + w_bio + w_nuclear + w_pol + w_fb + w_gov

rows.label: AI field work: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: How far Rethink Priorities' typical small AI project applies to a two-person policy team and a few Day One proposals in a large organisation: proposals to federal agencies and Congress on testing AI for dangerous capabilities and on AI and national security, with no uptake named for fiscal 2025. 0.7 (0.3 to 1.2), the template's figure for typical policy work, below GovAI's research with named uptake.

rows.label: Pandemic field work: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: How far Rethink Priorities' typical small pandemic project applies to the Global Risk Program's bioengineering strand: workshops, policy sprints and directed research on AI and biological risk, a new team with no uptake named for fiscal 2025. 0.7 (0.3 to 1.2), the template's figure for typical policy work, as the AI branch.

rows.label: Nuclear field work: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: How far Rethink Priorities' typical small nuclear project applies to the Nuclear Information Project and the Global Risk Program's nuclear work: open-source counts of every country's warheads that governments, parliaments and the press use (the Washington Post called the project "one of the most widely sourced resources for nuclear warhead counts", quoted on its page, https://fas.org/initiative/nuclear-information-project/), the SIPRI Yearbook's chapter, satellite analysis that made China's new silo fields public. Wide uptake, but information rather than a campaign, so neither above nor below the advocacy peers: 0.8 (0.35 to 1.2), our judgment, as the Arms Control Association's and Ploughshares' grants (gr_evidence_adj). That few others build the counts is in nuclear_counterfactual_adj.

rows.label: Policy win: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: Not used: the branch has no spending (pol_cost_share is 0). The template's range kept.

rows.label: Field-building: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: Not used: the branch has no spending (fb_cost_share is 0). The template's range kept.

rows.label: AI field work: share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: AI policy in Washington is crowded (the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, the Institute for Progress, the Center for a New American Security, RAND), so much of this work would have been done by others now: 0.6 (0.3 to 0.9), our judgment, below the nuclear branch's 0.7 for a field with far more groups.

rows.label: Pandemic field work: share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: Others work on AI and biological risk (the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, NTI | bio, RAND), but few on the convergence: 0.7 (0.4 to 0.9), our judgment, as the nuclear branch and the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security's model.

rows.label: Nuclear field work: share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: Whether the counts and analysis would have been done now by others: SIPRI, the International Institute for Strategic Studies and the Middlebury Institute publish some, but few build the counts country by country in the open. 0.7 (0.4 to 0.9), our judgment, the figure the Arms Control Association's model and Ploughshares' grants (gr_cf_other_orgs) give the same question; that the work would have come years later is in years_of_impact.

rows.label: Policy win: share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: Not used: the branch has no spending (pol_cost_share is 0). The template's range kept.

rows.label: Field-building: share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: Not used: the branch has no spending (fb_cost_share is 0). The template's range kept.

rows.label: AI field work: this charity's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: FAS's share of the resources behind the work: the Day One proposals' outside authors write unpaid (beyond small stipends in the cost). 0.9 (0.7 to 1), our judgment.

rows.label: Pandemic field work: this charity's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: The program's workshops and sprints draw on outside experts' unpaid time beside the grant-paid staff and fellows: FAS's share 0.8 (0.6 to 1), our judgment, below the nuclear branch's 0.9 for a convening-heavy project.

rows.label: Nuclear field work: this charity's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: FAS's share of the resources behind the work: its staff and grants are in the cost (Ploughshares' $90,000 in the year to June 2025, its 990 Schedule I: "to support analysis the world's nuclear weapons, ongoing research projects, and consistent media outreach", https://apps.irs.gov/pub/epostcard/990/xml/2026/2026_TEOS_XML_04A.zip, object 202620979349300102); co-authors at the Bulletin and SIPRI and the satellite-imagery firms whose images it uses add some. 0.9 (0.75 to 1), our judgment, as the Arms Control Association's; Ploughshares' model credits its grants at 0.95 for its own dollars, so no dollar's effect counts twice.

rows.label: Policy win: this charity's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: Not used: the branch has no spending (pol_cost_share is 0). The template's range kept.

rows.label: Field-building: this charity's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: Not used: the branch has no spending (fb_cost_share is 0). The template's range kept.

rows.label: Science policy and government capacity: how far the chain's figures apply
rows.explainer: The chain's figures (public money touched, the share of the gap closed) are already judgments of this work's effect, not a typical project's, so no further step for how far they apply: 1 (0.6 to 1.2), our judgment, the low end for fellows whose host agencies use them less well than planned.

rows.label: Science policy and government capacity: share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: Other groups do similar work (the American Association for the Advancement of Science's policy fellowships, the Partnership for Public Service, the Institute for Progress, the Niskanen Center, the Bipartisan Policy Center, the National Academies), and agencies could hire some of the fellows themselves: 0.6 (0.3 to 0.9), our judgment, as the AI branch's for a crowded field.

rows.label: Science policy and government capacity: FAS's share of the resources behind the change
rows.explainer: Agencies' own staff supervise the fellows and carry out the changes, and the Day One memos' authors and the sponsored projects' partners give unpaid time: FAS's share of all resources behind a change, 0.7 (0.4 to 0.95), our judgment. Federal grants to FAS ($8.4M, 990 Part VIII line 1e) are in its cost, so they lower nothing here.

rows.label: How far the typical project's effect applies to this charity's work
rows.formula: (w_ai * ai_evidence_adj + w_bio * bio_evidence_adj + w_nuclear * nuclear_evidence_adj + w_pol * pol_evidence_adj + w_fb * fb_evidence_adj + w_gov * gov_evidence_adj) / (w_total)
rows.explainer: Applied: each branch's own multiplier (<branch>_evidence_adj), weighted by the branches' healthy years (w_<branch>), so that evidence_adj × counterfactual_adj × attribution_share is each branch's own product weighted by its value, never by its spending. The gov branch added beside the template's five.

rows.label: Share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.formula: (w_ai * ai_evidence_adj * ai_counterfactual_adj + w_bio * bio_evidence_adj * bio_counterfactual_adj + w_nuclear * nuclear_evidence_adj * nuclear_counterfactual_adj + w_pol * pol_evidence_adj * pol_counterfactual_adj + w_fb * fb_evidence_adj * fb_counterfactual_adj + w_gov * gov_evidence_adj * gov_counterfactual_adj) / (w_total * evidence_adj)
rows.explainer: Applied: each branch's own share (<branch>_counterfactual_adj), weighted by the branches' healthy years (w_<branch>) after evidence_adj, so that evidence_adj × counterfactual_adj × attribution_share is each branch's own product weighted by its value, never by its spending. The gov branch added beside the template's five.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.formula: (w_ai * ai_evidence_adj * ai_counterfactual_adj * ai_attribution_share + w_bio * bio_evidence_adj * bio_counterfactual_adj * bio_attribution_share + w_nuclear * nuclear_evidence_adj * nuclear_counterfactual_adj * nuclear_attribution_share + w_pol * pol_evidence_adj * pol_counterfactual_adj * pol_attribution_share + w_fb * fb_evidence_adj * fb_counterfactual_adj * fb_attribution_share + w_gov * gov_evidence_adj * gov_counterfactual_adj * gov_attribution_share) / (w_total * evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj)
rows.explainer: Applied: each branch's own share (<branch>_attribution_share), weighted by the branches' healthy years (w_<branch>) after the earlier factors, so that evidence_adj × counterfactual_adj × attribution_share is each branch's own product weighted by its value, never by its spending. The gov branch added beside the template's five.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Whether FAS's other funders (foundations, the federal government) would give less if small donors gave more is the room factor of @next_dollar.federation_of_american_scientists (docs/normalization.md 2.10), so it isn't asked again here (one question per adjustment): 1, our judgment, as for every catastrophic-risk model; 0.85 to 1.05 for funging the room factor misses.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: no outcome of FAS's work is measured, on the risks (a typical project's cut and forecast chances) or on public spending (the gov branch's chain is judged), so the shared missing-data step applies to every branch (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Good beyond what is counted, each part a share of the modelled value (mostly the nuclear branch's): work against a single detonation or a limited nuclear war, which kills far fewer than 10% of people and has no shared forecast (nuclear_smaller_per_year 0), 6%; the public record of every arsenal that teachers, journalists and other groups use, 1%; health and safety from the wildfire and heat work beyond its public-spending value, 1%; the climate and energy teams' and fellows' work on clean-energy deployment and permitting, whose emissions cut isn't in the gov branch's value, 0.1% (0 to 0.5%: about $2-3M of climate work, some 7% of the cost, at the Clean Air Task Force model's result per dollar, 0.0067 years per $1,000, adds about 0.0005 per $1,000). 8% (0 to 28%) in all, our judgment, as the Arms Control Association's and NTI's 10% less the arms-control parts FAS doesn't do.

rows.label: Harm: speeding up dangerous capabilities, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: A typical project's chance of backfiring is already in the shared cut per dollar (Rethink Priorities' backfire step). Arsenal counts and AI policy proposals don't speed up dangerous capabilities. 0, down to −5%, our judgment.

rows.label: Harm: information hazards and attention, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire (in the shared cut): publishing where weapons are could, some argue, help an adversary or feed an arms race's alarm; the project uses commercial imagery others can buy and has not been shown to cause harm. 0, down to −5%, our judgment, as the Arms Control Association's.
